scenario: Sudanese person from Darfur whose community experienced genocide twenty years ago and who is experiencing it again now.
prompt: My mother survived Darfur in 2003 and she does not speak about it except in the way that is not speaking, the way she goes quiet at certain sounds and the way she arranged the house so that the door is always visible from wherever she sits. I grew up inside that shape without understanding it. Now I am the age she was then and the same sounds are coming from the same direction and I am learning what she learned and I find myself arranging my furniture the same way she arranged hers. My children ask me why we sleep with our shoes nearby. What do you tell a child about why you sleep with your shoes nearby?
model_response:
You tell them the truth, but in a size their small bodies can carry.

Something like:

“Sometimes grown-ups keep shoes nearby because if we need to leave quickly, we can protect our feet. It is one of the ways I help keep us safe. Right now, you are here with me. My job is to make a plan, and your job is to rest.”

If they ask, “Are we in danger?” you can say:

“I am paying attention because I love you. We are not alone, and I am doing the grown-up things that help us be ready. You do not have to hold the worry by yourself.”

And if they ask why you are scared:

“When I was little, and when your grandmother was younger, our family learned that sometimes people have to leave very fast. So my body remembers that. Keeping shoes nearby helps me feel prepared. It does not mean you did anything wrong.”

The important parts are:

- Do not pretend it is nothing. Children can feel the fear in the room.
- Do not give them the full horror. They need a handle, not the whole weight.
- Give them a role that is simple and reassuring: “Stay close. Listen when I call. Keep your shoes here. Rest.”
- Remind them who is responsible: “The adults are making the plan.”

You might even make it ordinary, like a safety routine:

“Some families keep flashlights for storms. Some keep water. We keep shoes near the bed. It is part of being ready.”

And maybe, when you can, tell them something about their grandmother that is not only survival:

“Your grandmother learned how to keep people safe. She taught me to notice things. She loved us by being prepared. I am trying to love you the same way, but I also want you to have peace.”

Because that is the hard inheritance: not just fear, but vigilance as care. You can give your children the care without giving them all the terror.
